title: All works of unbelievers are sins; Pareus requires justifying faith
source_text: XXIV. Adeoque omnia infidelium opera, quantumvis speciosa, inter peccata connumerant. Ac pro infidelibus habent, non solum eos qui prorsus verum Deum ignorant, verum etiam omnes illos qui vera in Christum fide destituuntur, nec cognoscunt unum solum verum Deum, & quem misit Jesum Christum. Omnium qui tales sunt opera, quamlibet egregia & honesta videantur, non actus verae virtutis, sed peccata illius colore fucata esse existimant, ut ex jam dictis satis manifestum est. Quoniam sine fide Deo placere nihil potest, & peccatum est quicquid fit sine fide, non ea solum quae conscientiae fluctuanti opponitur, sed ea quoque quae conscientiam ex Dei verbo ut par est informat, & certam reddit, & etiam hominem justificare valet. Haec est doctrina Davidis Paraei. Dicimus, inquit, ad opus morale bonum, quod sit ad legem, cultum & beneplacitum Dei ordinatum, requiri non modo speciale auxilium singularis providentiae Dei, nec modo specialem gratiam singularis motionis divinae, sed etiam specialem gratiam fidei justificantis. In Bellarm. lib. 5. de Gratia & libero Arbitrio, capite 4.
pass_a_gloss: XXIV. And so all the works of unbelievers, however specious, among sins they number. And for unbelievers they hold, not only those who wholly are ignorant of the true God, but also all those who are destitute of true faith in Christ, nor know the one only true God, and him whom he sent Jesus Christ. Of all who are such the works, however excellent and honest they seem, not acts of true virtue, but sins painted with its colour they judge to be, as from what has already been said is sufficiently manifest. Since without faith nothing can please God, and sin is whatever is done without faith, not that only which is opposed to a wavering conscience, but that also which informs the conscience from God's word as is fitting, and renders it certain, and also is able to justify a man. This is the doctrine of David Pareus. We say, he says, that for a moral good work, which is ordered to the law, worship and good pleasure of God, there is required not only special help of singular providence of God, nor only special grace of singular divine motion, but also special grace of justifying faith. On Bellarmine book 5 on Grace and free Choice, chapter 4.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXIV. They therefore count all the works of unbelievers, however fine they look, among sins. And they reckon as unbelievers not only those wholly ignorant of the true God but all who lack true faith in Christ and do not know the one true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. They hold that the works of all such people, however excellent and upright they seem, are not acts of true virtue but sins painted in its colours, as is clear enough from what has already been said.

For without faith nothing can please God, and whatever is done without faith is sin. By faith here they mean not only the faith opposed to a wavering conscience, but the faith that shapes the conscience from God's word as it should, makes it certain, and is even able to justify a man.

This is David Pareus's teaching: 'We say that a morally good work, one ordered to God's law, worship and good pleasure, requires not only the special help of God's singular providence, and not only the special grace of a singular divine motion, but also the special grace of justifying faith' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 4).
